title: Otis and the Gloomberry Mystery
markdown:
Nestled in a valley so green it sparkled lay Willowbrook, and in Willowbrook lived Otis: a young wizard with hair the colour of toasted hazelnuts, forever escaping as if eager to explore. His nose twitched with curiosity. He could make teacups dance a merry jig. He could even make socks sort themselves, though the red ones always tangled with the blue. He dreamt of dragons and faraway lands, and mostly he enjoyed the small magic that made a day a little more special.

The most exciting day of the year was the annual Summer Fair. Bunting sagged between cottages. Someone had spelled the bunting to flutter even when the wind forgot. Stalls piled with jam tarts that smelled like sunshine in a jar. A swing so high you could almost tickle the clouds. A fiddler played a tune that kept losing its own ending and starting again, cheerfully. Otis’s pockets jingled with a few carefully saved copper coins. He bought nothing yet. He was particularly excited about Ring the Pixie’s Nose: skill, a little luck, and a grand prize whispered about in delighted tones. Last year the prize had been a spoon that stirred itself. This year the stall was hung with a curtain, which meant the prize was trying to be a surprise.

A flick of the wrist. A whisper: “Hocus Pocus Focus!” The wooden ring sailed, a perfect arc, and landed with a satisfying clink around the longest, pointiest pixie nose you ever did see.

The stallholder, a jovial man whose belly jiggled like unset jelly, clapped. “Well done, young wizard!” From under the table—a place rumoured to hold wonders—he pulled a ball of woolly fluff the size of a plump rabbit, two large curious ears, a tail that wagged as if it had heard the funniest joke in the world.

“He’s a woolly dog?” Otis had imagined something more wizardly.

“A rare breed. Loves to chase moonbeams and chew on dandelion roots. Name him what you will.”

Otis patted the fluff. A velvety nose nudged his hand. Warmth. “Mairi,” he declared. “You shall be Mairi.” The tail wagged so hard the whole body wiggled, a furry exclamation point.

That evening the moon, a silver coin in the inky sky, began its climb. From the cozy kitchen, Otis’s grandmother called, voice warm as a freshly baked biscuit. “Could you fetch me some moonpetal herbs from the edge of the Whispering Woods? For my sleepy-time tea. The finest ones grow there.”

An ordinary errand: a quick dash and back. Mairi was no ordinary pet. At the word woods, ears perked, a happy little woof. He seemed to know exactly where he was going.

“Are you sure, Mairi?” A tremor. Even in daylight the Whispering Woods made ancient trees rustle tales you could not quite understand. At night, stranger things. Shadows danced. Leaves sounded like hushed conversations.

Mairi trotted ahead anyway, fluffy tail a beacon in the gathering dusk. Otis followed, copper coins still in his pocket, unused, which felt like a kind of bravery. Leaves turned like pages of an old book. The path was barely there, moon-lit, fireflies like fallen stars among the ferns. An owl asked a question and did not wait for an answer. Mairi sniffed moss, chased flicker-lights, padded softly. He was not fazed. Once he stopped so suddenly Otis nearly walked into a woolly backside. Mairi had found a dandelion root and considered it, then left it, as if the woods deserved to keep a few of their own jokes.

They came to a small clearing where moonpetals unfurled, white petals glowing pearly. Otis paused. Wonder. He reached—and a gruff voice snapped like a twig.

“Oi! What are you doing in my berry patch? Get out of it!”

On a mossy stump, pointy green hat askew: a goblin, small, long tangled beard like a bird’s nest after a storm, eyes darting. A basket of plump dark berries shimmered with an unusual rainbow-coloured glow. This was Grizelda, the goblin berry seller, not known for a sunny disposition.

“Oh! Excuse me, sir.” Otis stammered. “Moonpetal herbs. For my grandmother’s tea.”

“Moonpetals, eh?” A squint. “Those grow near my prize-winning Gloomberries. You’ll scare off the dew sprites if you go poking about. Very sensitive.”

Some of the Gloomberries looked a little sad. Not shimmering as they should. Deep purple faded. “Your berries don’t look very happy.”

Grizelda’s mottled green turned a deeper emerald. “Of course they don’t look happy! They’re Gloomberries! They’re supposed to look gloomy! It’s their name! You young wizards and your notions!”

“Maybe they’re sad because they’re lonely.” He remembered his grandmother saying even plants liked company, in their quiet way. Mairi sniffed the edge of the basket, ears forward.

“Lonely?” A snort like a small unhappy pig. “Berries don’t get lonely. They sit. Being gloomy. It’s what they do best.”

“Mairi loves company. He’s never lonely.” As if on cue, a happy little bark, a fluffy head nudged Grizelda’s grubby green leg.

She blinked. Soft. Gentle. Not stealing. Not yapping. Friendly. Remarkably fluffy. “Well, I never. A dog that isn’t trying to chase me or eat my wares. Usually they just want my berries.”

“What if Mairi just sits with them a little while? Perhaps their gloominess will rub off. Or his fluffiness will cheer them up.”

Grizelda looked at the berries, faint shimmer dimming with her doubt. Then at the earnest wizard, the gentle dog. “You think a woolly creature will cheer up my berries?” Wonder creeping into the gruff.

“It’s worth a try.”

A long sigh, wind in a hollow log. She set the basket on the moss. Mairi, with surprising dignity for a creature made of fluff, curled up beside it. Warm wool. He did not eat a single berry. He lay there, peaceful, as if sitting were a spell and he had practised.

They waited. Otis did not poke. Grizelda did not poke. A dew sprite, if there was one, stayed hidden, which was its job. The Gloomberries perked. The dark iridescent shimmer grew a little brighter, first at the rim of the basket, then toward the middle, like a blush. A faint sweet scent, like moonlight distilled. Grizelda leaned in, beard bristling, and sniffed as if she might catch the berries being cheerful in the act.

“Well, I’ll be a toadstool!” Grumbling forgotten. “They are looking better! Brighter, even!” A small goblin-sized smile, rare. “Alright, young wizard. You can have your moonpetals. And you can keep that fluffy thing. He’s good for the berries.”

Otis gathered the fragrant moonpetals quickly, thanked her. A curt nod, sour expression softened. Homeward: Mairi proud, tail high. The woods no longer felt like an argument. Moonlight was kind. Leaves rustled like a lullaby.

Grandmother was delighted, eyes twinkling. She crumbled a moonpetal into the pot and the kitchen smelled like night that had decided to be kind. Mairi curled by the crackling hearth, a contented sigh, tail thump-thump on the warm rug. Otis stroked the incredibly soft fur. The fair prize had not been wizardly. It had been better. The tea, when it was poured, smelled of moonpetals and a little of wool, which Grandmother did not mention, which was a kindness too. She did mention that the red socks had tangled with the blue again, and Otis, for once, let them.
characters: Otis (young wizard), Mairi (woolly dog), Grizelda (goblin berry seller)
